arguments.concept: Addition joins two groups into one total. Start from one number and count on by the other number.
When a sum passes ten, make ten first. Split the second number so that one part completes ten, then add the rest.
Subtraction asks how far apart two numbers are. Use the matching addition fact: the smaller number plus the difference gives the larger number.
To subtract from a teen number, go back to ten first. Take away the ones of the teen number, then take away what is left of the subtrahend.

steps: You have taken away $6$, and $9 = 6 + 3$, so $3$ is still left to take away.

arguments.concept: A multiplication fact counts equal groups. When a fact is not yet automatic, build it from a nearby fact you know, for example by doubling.

steps: $8$ is twice $4$, so double the product: $28 + 28 = 56$.

arguments.concept: Facts with $11$ or $12$ split into a ten part and a small part. Multiply each part, then add the two products.
Division undoes multiplication. Ask which number multiplied by the divisor gives the dividend.

steps: Ask which number multiplied by $6$ gives $54$.

arguments.concept: A missing factor is found by division. Divide the product by the factor you know.

steps: The box is the number that $7$ multiplies to give $21$.

arguments.concept: A square multiplies a number by itself. The small raised $2$ tells you to use the base twice as a factor.
A perfect square is a whole number times itself. To test a number, compare it with the squares near it; if it sits strictly between two consecutive squares, it is not a perfect square.

steps: $75$ is larger than $64$ and smaller than $81$, so no whole number squared gives $75$.
Check: $75$ lies strictly between $64$ and $81$, so it is not a perfect square.

arguments.concept: Each digit has a place, and the place sets its value. Read the places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands.

worked_example.problem: What is the value of the $6$ in $2{,}613$?
steps: Name the places from the right: $3$ ones, $1$ ten, $6$ hundreds, $2$ thousands.
The digit $6$ sits in the hundreds place.
A $6$ in the hundreds place is worth $6 \times 100$.

arguments.concept: Expanded form writes a number as the sum of its place values. A zero digit adds nothing, so leave it out of the sum.

steps: Read each digit with its place: $3$ ten-thousands, $0$ thousands, $7$ hundreds, $0$ tens, $2$ ones.
Write the value of each nonzero digit: $30000$, $700$, and $2$.
Join the values with plus signs.

arguments.concept: A number with more digits is larger. When two numbers have the same number of digits, compare place by place from the left; the first place where the digits differ decides.

steps: Both numbers have four digits, so compare from the left.
Thousands: $7$ and $7$, equal. Hundreds: $3$ and $3$, equal.
Tens: $1$ and $8$. Since $8 > 1$, the second number is larger.

arguments.concept: To order numbers, compare them place by place from the left. Pick the least number, then repeat with the numbers that remain.

steps: All three numbers have three digits, so compare the hundreds digits: $8$, $2$, $4$.
The smallest hundreds digit is $2$, so $284$ comes first. Next is $4$, so $428$ is second. Last is $8$, so $842$ is third.

arguments.concept: To round, look at the digit just to the right of the target place. If it is $5$ or more, round the target digit up; if it is $4$ or less, keep the target digit. Then replace every digit to the right with $0$.

steps: The tens digit is $7$. The digit to its right, the ones digit, is $6$.
$6$ is $5$ or more, so round the tens digit up from $7$ to $8$.

arguments.concept: Rounding to a larger place uses the same rule: look at the digit just right of the target place. A $5$ in that spot always rounds up, even when nothing follows it.

steps: The thousands digit is $8$. The digit to its right is $2$.
$2$ is less than $5$, so the thousands digit stays $8$.
Replace every digit to the right of the thousands place with $0$.
